story.intro: In 2025, our four-person team studied how patients and caregivers buy medicines. We developed three directions: a unified health card and app, a dispensing kiosk and RFID packaging. The report took the card/app further. The November 2026 continuation adds interface walkthroughs; the kiosk is a separate learning exercise, not a replacement for the selected concept.

outcome.title: Current outcome
outcome.text: We produced field research, service maps and three concept directions. The report developed a health card and app further. New November 2026 interface walkthroughs make collection and kiosk tasks reviewable. These are simulations; no participant evaluation, operational pilot, cost reduction or shorter wait has been demonstrated.

blocks.text: Patients and caregivers paying for medicines need reliable information about their options and prices. Our research found that prescription confusion and uncertain stock made it harder to plan an affordable purchase and could mean another visit.
We focused on this question: how could the service help people understand medicine options and prices, check availability and get support before they pay?
Notes behind stock and spending concerns

visuals.alt: Original supply-chain affinity cluster contains notes about stockouts, waiting, buying larger quantities and trying other medicines.
visuals.caption: Supply-chain affinity notes · Reported concerns about stockouts, waiting and availability informed the service direction. Original research excerpt, report p.29, Figure 44; these are research perceptions.

visuals.alt: Original medicine-spending affinity cluster groups notes about self-paying, recurring expense and difficulty affording medicines.
visuals.caption: Medicine-spending affinity notes · Recurring expense and self-paying emerged in the research. The budget example is an individual account, not a measured service saving. Report p.29, Figure 44.

visual.alt: Original selected problem statement links medicine spending with limited access to information about medicine options and prices.
visual.caption: Original problem framing · The team’s selected statement, report p.45. This frames the design challenge; it is not a measured kiosk outcome.

blocks.text: What the next service needs to address

items.title: Prescription confusion → a clear review
items.body: Keep prescription, medicine and permitted quantity together so someone can check what they are collecting. Unclear information still needs pharmacy help.

items.title: Stock uncertainty → verified availability
items.body: Show a reliable stock result before payment and explain unavailable items. Checking before travel still needs a channel beyond the on-site kiosk.

items.title: Help already matters → retain a handoff
items.body: Keep staff help visible when someone cannot identify a medicine, sign in or complete collection. An unattended machine cannot replace that support.

blocks.text: We visited Jan Aushadhi pharmacies and used observation, interviews and questionnaires to study medicine purchases. We included patients, caregivers and pharmacy teams, with questionnaires for users, non-users, pharmacy operators and doctors.
What the retained research can establish

items.title: Mapped purchase accounts
items.body: The contextual-inquiry models on report pages 14–17 show people, dependencies and purchase sequences. A caregiver account connects prescription-name confusion, price and contacting the pharmacy before travelling. These accounts explain a situation; they are not frequency estimates.

items.title: Four questionnaire groups
items.body: Pages 20–28 separate customers, non-users, Kendra operators and doctors. Recruitment details and a reliable response base for each chart could not be verified from the retained records. We do not turn their percentages into a participant total or combine them with the contextual accounts.

items.title: Research synthesis
items.body: The affinity map on page 29 groups reported stock, spending, awareness and trust concerns. We use those as research perceptions and design questions; comments about medicine quality are not clinical evidence.

blocks.text: In one mapped caregiver purchase, matching prescription names to medicines required help, and the pharmacy was contacted by phone or WhatsApp to check availability and opening times. The stockout sequence then led to waiting, another store or human help. Those accounts connected information clarity, availability and staff support in our design question.

blocks.text: We followed the purchase in context: how people understood the prescription, looked for medicine and handled a stockout. A Kendra is a Jan Aushadhi pharmacy.

visual.alt: Original Jan Aushadhi purchase sequence maps a medicine stockout to waiting for restocking, visiting another Kendra or asking about an alternative.
visual.caption: Mapped purchase sequence · Stockouts can mean waiting, another visit or an alternative. Original team map, report p.16, Figure 3.

blocks.text: Our research brought together confusion about prescription names, uncertain stock, repeat visits and trust in the service. These findings describe the purchase experience; they do not measure the effect of a new kiosk.

We mapped how patients and families depend on doctors, pharmacy staff and medicine suppliers. The maps show where information and responsibility pass between people, helping us identify what a kiosk alone could not solve.

visual.alt: Original contextual-inquiry flow model connects patients, family, clinicians, Kendras, pharmacies and medicine-supply actors.
visual.caption: Original service flow · People, information and purchase dependencies. Report p.14, Figure 1; annotations reflect the team’s research synthesis.

blocks.text: Who needs support, and who can act

visual.alt: Original stakeholder map groups patients, customers, doctors, Kendra operators and owners, manufacturers, government, warehouse and wider service actors.
visual.caption: Original stakeholder map · Patients, pharmacy teams and the organisations surrounding a purchase. These are service actors, rather than a recruitment count. Report p.18, Figure 5.

blocks.text: We also compared who needs the service with who can help it operate. Patients and caregivers need clear choices; pharmacy staff, suppliers and other organisations would need to support stock information and fulfilment.

visual.caption: Stakeholder priorities · The team’s power–interest analysis, report p.19, Figure 6.

sections.title: Service concepts
sections.limitation: The report contains proposed services and illustrative concept artwork. The later interface walkthroughs do not establish a deployed service or working dispensing hardware.

blocks.text: We generated fifteen early ideas and developed three directions: a unified health card and app, a dispensing kiosk, and RFID-enabled packaging. The report took the card/app direction further. The kiosk and packaging remain visible as explored alternatives, rather than being presented as rejected or proven inferior.

items.title: Unified health card and app
items.body: Selected for further development in the report.

items.title: Medicine-dispensing kiosk
items.body: Explored alternative; later interface-learning continuation.

items.title: RFID-enabled medicine packaging
items.body: Explored traceability concept.

blocks.text: Why develop a shared card and app?

The report connects the selected direction to keeping prescriptions together, making medicine information accessible and checking availability before a visit (pages 47 and 57–58). This is the proposed mechanism behind the choice, not evidence that it performed better than the alternatives.

items.title: Reach the decision before travel
items.body: The mapped purchase already involved contacting the pharmacy for availability. An app or another remote channel could support that earlier step; a machine at the pharmacy cannot solve it on its own.

items.title: Carry information between people
items.body: The proposed card links a patient account to doctor and pharmacy interactions. The packaging concept instead identifies a package record. Those are different service roles, so one is not a direct replacement for the other.

items.title: Accept the coordination cost
items.body: The card/app depends on reliable records, current stock and participating staff. Its broader feature list does not remove those dependencies. The present walkthrough therefore concentrates on checking and requesting collection, with other functions left as proposed scope.

blocks.text: Complete idea inventory from report p.46. These are early team proposals, not delivered features or demonstrated medical capabilities.

blocks.text: Unified health card and app

We proposed one route for keeping prescription information accessible, understanding medicine options and planning a collection. The report selected this direction and developed enrolment, doctor and pharmacy interactions. The next chapter shows its full proposed scope.
Medicine-dispensing kiosk

We explored a machine beside a pharmacy to guide identification, prescription selection, stock checks, payment and collection. It would still depend on reliable stock, staff support and clear recovery when a purchase fails. Its illustrations are concept artwork, not hardware photographs.

visual.alt: Two original kiosk concept illustrations: a close-up dispensing-machine proposal and a contextual hospital-corridor view.
visual.caption: Earlier kiosk illustrations · Original concept artwork, report p.48, Figures 64–65. These are unbuilt explorations, not hardware photographs.

visual.alt: Earlier unbuilt kiosk flow includes a QR card, OTP or biometric verification, prescription and stock checks, payment, dispensing and receipt paths.
visual.caption: Earlier kiosk alternative · Report p.49, Figure 66. QR and OTP/biometric verification belong to this unbuilt exploration. The report selected a health-card/app; my current continuation explores card/PIN identification.

blocks.text: The earlier flow considered missing prescriptions, unavailable stock, permitted quantities, retry/cancel and receipts. A kiosk at the pharmacy cannot by itself answer the question of availability before someone travels. That still needs a separate information channel.
RFID-enabled medicine packaging

We proposed a unique package identity linked to batch, expiry, billing and supporting quality records. The intended route was tagging, a recorded bill, and access through a shared link. The tag and the records behind it were not implemented; the illustration does not establish authenticity or medicine quality.

items.title: Inspect the fictional package-record example
items.note: New explanatory interaction · No tag reader or verified product record. It separates a record’s fields from evidence that a medicine is authentic.

visual.alt: Original concept illustration of a medicine carton and strips with package identity labels.
visual.caption: RFID packaging proposal · Report p.50, Figure67. Original illustrative artwork; no working tag or verified traceability system is demonstrated.

blocks.text: The report records the selected direction and its intended benefits, but no formal comparative test or complete selection deliberation. The three directions remain part of the project. My later kiosk exercise is a separate learning choice, explained in its own chapter.

We developed the unified health card and app further in the report. The card would identify the account; the app would bring prescription information, medicine details and collection planning together. These were proposed service functions, not a launched platform or measured improvement.

items.note: New November 2026 AI-assisted interface exploration. Prepared fictional data and a local collection request, not live inventory, a medical record or a confirmed reservation.

blocks.text: Three connected journeys

items.title: Join with help
items.body: A proposed registration centre checks documents and issues a physical or digital card. Consent and information requirements need review before real enrolment.

items.title: Keep the prescription available
items.body: The proposed doctor journey retrieves the permitted record and adds a prescription. It depends on consent, reliable records and staff access; no medical-record integration was built.

items.title: Plan collection
items.body: The proposed app checks medicine information and availability, then sends a collection request to the Kendra. The pharmacy prepares the order and helps with collection.

blocks.text: Where the service still needs a person

items.title: An availability result needs an owner
items.body: The source pharmacy flow assigns stock checking to the operator. A real pre-travel result would need someone responsible for its accuracy and freshness. The new walkthrough supplies fictional results; an unknown result routes to help.

items.title: A request is not a reservation
items.body: The walkthrough creates a local reference awaiting store review. Staff would need to agree who receives it, when they confirm it and whether stock is held before anyone travels. No request in this prototype contacts a pharmacy.

items.title: The handoff must be completed
items.body: The source flow places prescription review, stock checks and fulfilment with pharmacy staff. Passing a reference to the help screen only marks that dependency; it does not mean staff accepted the request or authorised collection.

blocks.text: What the card and app were intended to contain

items: AI-assisted prescription reading and quantity suggestion

blocks.text: The source also proposes AI-assisted reading and quantity calculation. These functions were not implemented or evaluated. The new walkthrough uses prepared fictional items and fixed limits; it does not interpret a prescription or recommend a medicine.

These substantial first-use requirements need revision and staff review; this is a present design judgment, not a finding validated by this project. sections.title: Kiosk learning exploration

steps.title: Use the prepared account
steps.body: The lab models card/PIN entry with a demo action. It never asks for a real card or PIN. Someone without access can request staff help.

steps.title: Review the prepared items
steps.body: Choose fictional items within fixed limits and check the simulated stock result before payment.

steps.title: Review and simulate payment
steps.body: Edit quantities without losing the selection. Pending or unknown payment keeps the same reference while the result is checked.

steps.title: Collect or get help
steps.body: A confirmed result can lead to collection. Missing stock, uncertain payment or failed collection has a staff-supported route; no machine actually dispenses anything.

sections.limitation: Identity, prescriptions, items, stock, payment and collection are simulated. No real financial transaction, medical recommendation, wallet service or dispensing is connected.

blocks.text: I chose a separate kiosk interface exercise because I had less experience designing for that format and wanted to broaden my design perspective. The new November 2026 AI-assisted prototype models a prepared account, prescription selection, stock review, simulated payment and collection or help. It is separate from our original team’s selected card/app concept.

items.title: Try the separate kiosk interface exploration
items.note: Later learning exercise · New AI-assisted November 2026 prototype. All identity, stock, payment and collection states are simulated; not evaluated with participants.

blocks.text: We produced field research, service maps and three concept directions, then developed the unified card/app further in our report. The later interface walkthroughs make a bounded part of the service reviewable. Next, pharmacy staff need to check the assumptions, followed by patient/caregiver sessions and revisions. No improvement in cost or waiting time has been measured.
A lesson from the mapped purchase

The caregiver sequence already used phone or WhatsApp contact to check a pharmacy before travelling. That account gives the current continuation a concrete priority: make the stock result, request status and staff handoff understandable before adding more account or AI functions. This is a present design judgment grounded in that source account, not a newly observed improvement.

items.title: Review the concepts with pharmacy staff
items.body: Compare the card/app, kiosk and package-identity roles. Check stock ownership, staff handoffs, permitted collection and the reliability of each information source.

items.title: Evaluate the selected journey
items.body: Observe patients and caregivers using the prepared card/app collection task. Keep concept comprehension, interface usability and the separate kiosk learning tasks distinct.

items.title: Operational evaluation
items.body: A later pilot would need to examine stock accuracy, fulfilment, staff workload, purchase time and actual spending against a baseline.

items.title: What I learned
items.body: A cheaper medicine is only useful if someone can understand the options, find it in stock and get help when needed. Those service gaps need attention alongside the kiosk screen.
